props.title: The Untouchables

sections.content: Brian De Palma's The Untouchables (1987) revolutionized gangster cinema by infusing Prohibition-era Chicago with operatic grandeur. The film's most iconic sequence - the Union Station steps shootout - directly homages Eisenstein's Battleship Potemkin (1925) while creating something entirely fresh. De Palma's virtuoso direction, combined with David Mamet's razor-sharp screenplay, elevated what could have been a standard cops-vs-gangsters tale into high tragedy. The film stands alongside Once Upon a Time in America (1984) and Miller's Crossing (1990) as a masterwork that both honors and transcends classic gangster film conventions.

sections.content: De Palma's stylistic flourishes in The Untouchables draw from his extensive crime film vocabulary. The elaborate tracking shots and dramatic angles echo his work in Dressed to Kill (1980) and Body Double (1984), while the violence carries the operatic intensity he'd perfect later in Carlito's Way (1993). Robert De Niro's portrayal of Al Capone builds on the method intensity he brought to Goodfellas (1990), creating a villain of Shakespearean proportions.

The film's influence resonates through modern crime cinema. You can see its DNA in the period detail of Road to Perdition (2002), the moral complexity of L.A. Confidential (1997), and the team dynamics of The Departed (2006). Ennio Morricone's sweeping score created a template for how music can elevate crime drama to epic status. sections.content: The Untouchables marked a crucial shift in how Hollywood approached historical crime narratives. While earlier films like Bonnie and Clyde (1967) romanticized outlaws, De Palma's film focused on law enforcement's moral crusade. This influence can be traced through Public Enemies (2009) and Gangster Squad (2013), though neither achieved The Untouchables' perfect balance of historical drama and mythmaking.
